runs.x: Much of chemistry depends on careful observation, and the most useful observations are those that can be expressed with numbers. A doctor recording a patient’s temperature, a pharmacist preparing a dose of medicine and a chemist weighing out a sample all rely on measurements. For a measurement to be meaningful, it must be reported in a way that others can understand.
– a number-based description of something, made by comparing it to a standard
– the standard being used (what kind of quantity, and what size)
A number without a unit tells you nothing.
Ex: “the sample is 24”: 24 grams? 24 milliliters? 24 degrees?

A measurement is only useful if others can understand and repeat it. In 1999, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one engineering team reported its data in English units while another team expected metric units. To prevent errors like this, scientists around the world have agreed to use a single set of units.
– the set of units used by scientists around the world.
Using the same units lets everyone’s measurements be compared.
The SI is based on the
– one of the basic SI units that all other units are built from. These are the base units you will use in chemistry:
– a unit made by combining base units.
Use these symbols when you write measurements.
The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram, but in the chemistry lab we usually measure mass in grams (g).

Chemists measure objects across an enormous range of sizes, from the length of a lab bench to the width of a single atom. Atoms are so small that their radii are measured in picometers, trillionths of a meter. Regardless of size, each of these is a measurement of length.

Every object, from a grain of sand to a planet, is made of matter. The amount of that matter determines how heavy an object is and how difficult it is to move. In the lab, mass is one of the most common measurements a chemist will take.

All matter takes up space. That space can be as large as the water in a swimming pool or as small as the few milliliters of medicine in a syringe. Liquids in particular are almost always measured by the amount of space they occupy.

Temperature is one of the most important conditions in any chemistry lab. It determines whether a substance is a solid, liquid or gas, and it affects how quickly chemical reactions take place. This is why food is kept in a refrigerator: lower temperatures slow the reactions that cause food to spoil.

Every change in matter, from ice melting to fuel burning, involves energy. The energy stored in food is listed on nutrition labels in Calories, and the energy released by burning gasoline is what moves a car.
Atoms and molecules are far too small to count one by one. A single drop of water contains roughly 1.7 × 10
water molecules. In the same way that eggs are counted by the dozen and paper by the ream, chemists count particles in large groups.

runs.x: Although light is a form of energy, it has the ability to interact with matter. Light is often produced in chemical reactions and can be used to trigger certain chemical changes. The light emitted by atoms and molecules can even be used to identify them. Therefore, it is important that we understand what light is.
It is sometimes referred to as an Electromagnetic Wave.
Light waves are ripples in electric and magnetic fields.
is a single packet, or quantum, of light energy.
Light of specific energies can interact with the electrons in an atom.

Light can be described in the same way as the ripples that spread across a pond when a stone is dropped into it. Like any wave, each type of light can be described by measuring its size and how often it repeats.
All light waves can be described using 2 properties, wavelength and frequency
– the length of a single wave cycle, measured from crest to crest or trough to trough.

Every radio station is identified by a number, such as 101.1 FM. That number is the frequency at which the station broadcasts, in millions of cycles per second. Frequency is one of the most important ways of describing any wave, including light.
– the number of wave cycles that are completed in 1 second.
Picture standing still while waves pass you: frequency is how many crests go by each second.
Sunburns are caused by ultraviolet light, not visible light, even though both come from the sun. This is because different types of light carry different amounts of energy.
The frequency and wavelength of a light wave determine its energy
Higher-energy radiation (ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays) can damage living cells and DNA. Lower-energy radiation (visible light, infrared, microwaves) is mostly absorbed as heat.

Visible light is only a small part of a much larger family of light waves. Radio waves carry signals to phones and radios, microwaves heat food and X-rays allow doctors to see inside the body. All of these are forms of light that differ in their energy.

runs.x: One of a chemist’s greatest tools in studying matter is the Periodic Table of Elements. Understanding how to read this table reveals numerous patterns in element characteristics and reactivity. One of the first widely used periodic tables was developed by a chemist named Dmitri Mendeleev, who saw that when elements were placed in order of increasing atomic mass, their characteristics repeated themselves.

– molecules with an uneven (asymmetrical) distribution of charge. They have a partially positive end and a partially negative end.
– molecules with a symmetrical distribution of charge. They do not have a partially positive end and a partially negative end.

– possessing the same features on opposite sides of a molecule.
– possessing different features on opposite sides of a molecule.
Symmetry refers to the property of having matching features on opposite sides of a molecule.
In order for a molecule to be considered symmetrical, it must possess symmetry across each side of the molecule (top vs. bottom, left vs. right, etc.).

Molecules are attracted to one another by weak forces that arise due to differences in charge. These are known as intermolecular forces of attraction.
They are much weaker than the

sections.title: Strength of Intermolecular Forces of Attraction

runs.x: There are different types of intermolecular forces, and they can be differentiated by strength.
Recall that ions are atoms which possess a whole-number charge. Dipoles are polar molecules that have partially charged sides, one positive and one negative.
When brought together, ions and dipoles will exert an attractive force on one another.
– attractive force between an ion and the oppositely charged end of a polar molecule.
Found in mixtures of ionic and polar compounds.

Hydrogen has the capacity to form highly polar bonds when combined with oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine atoms, which are very electronegative. When molecules containing these bonds are brought together, there will be a strong attraction between them. This is known as a hydrogen bond.
– strong intermolecular force between molecules that contain hydrogen bonded to a very electronegative element (oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine).
Note that a hydrogen “bond” is not a chemical bond but rather an attraction
Found in compounds containing H + O, N or F.
When two polar molecules are brought together, their oppositely charged ends will attract. This is known as a dipole–dipole force.
– force of attraction between oppositely charged ends of polar molecules.

Atoms and molecules with a symmetrical charge distribution can still apply an attractive force on each other. As electrons “move” around the atom, temporary charges can form around even nonpolar molecules, due to the brief uneven distribution of electron density. Attractive forces can arise due to these temporary charges. We call these forces London dispersion forces.
– attraction between molecules due to temporary shifts in electron density that cause momentary dipoles.
Sometimes referred to as a van der Waals force, although that term technically includes hydrogen bonding, dipole–dipole forces and London dispersion forces.
The size of an atom or molecule has an impact on the strength of its London dispersion forces.
Larger atoms/molecules have bigger electron clouds whose valence electrons are further from the nucleus and more easily moved around. This leads to a higher probability of temporary dipoles forming.

Rubbing alcohol spread on the skin evaporates much faster than water. The strength of the attractions between particles determines how easily a liquid boils, holds together at its surface, flows and dissolves other substances.
The stronger the intermolecular forces in a substance, the more energy it takes to pull its particles apart.

To compare two substances, first find the strongest type of IFA in each (ion–dipole > hydrogen bonding > dipole–dipole > London dispersion). If both have the same type, compare size: larger molecules have stronger London forces.
To melt a solid or boil a liquid, the particles must gain enough energy to pull away from each other. Only the attractions
molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.
– the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. It is the same temperature at which the liquid freezes.
– the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout the liquid. It is the same temperature at which the gas condenses.
Stronger IFAs → higher melting and boiling points.
Weaker IFAs → lower melting and boiling points.
These substances are often gases at room temperature.

Inside a liquid, each molecule is pulled equally in all directions by its neighbors. At the surface, molecules are pulled only sideways and inward, so the surface acts like a stretched skin.
– the tendency of a liquid’s surface to hold together and resist being broken.
Water’s hydrogen bonds let it bead up into tall drops and let small insects walk on it.
These liquids spread out into flat puddles.
Viscous liquids (high viscosity) flow slowly. Ex: honey, glycerol
Nonviscous liquids (low viscosity) flow easily. Ex: hexane, water
For a liquid to flow, its molecules must slide past each other. Strong attractions hold the molecules in place, so the liquid flows slowly.
Glycerol has three O–H groups per molecule, so each molecule forms many hydrogen bonds.
Hexane molecules attract each other only weakly, so hexane flows easily.
Molecule size matters too: very long molecules (like those in vegetable oil) tangle together and have strong London forces overall, so oil is more viscous than water even though it is nonpolar.
– how much of a substance (the solute) can dissolve in another substance (the solvent).
A solute dissolves when the solvent’s particles attract the solute’s particles strongly enough to pull them away from each other.
– polar substances and ionic compounds dissolve in polar solvents like water. Nonpolar substances dissolve in nonpolar solvents like hexane.

the partial charges of water molecules pull the charged ions apart. The δ− oxygen ends attract the positive ions, and the δ+ hydrogen ends attract the negative ions (ion–dipole forces). Water molecules surround each ion and carry it into the solution.

the δ− end of a polar solute molecule attracts the δ+ hydrogen ends of water molecules, and the δ+ end of the solute attracts the δ− oxygen ends of water. These attractions pull the solute molecules away from each other and into the solution.
Ex: sugar has O–H groups, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with water molecules and dissolve.

polar water molecules have little attraction for nonpolar molecules, so they cannot pull them apart. Water molecules stay attracted to each other (hydrogen bonds), and the nonpolar substance stays separate.
Ex: oil and water do not mix; they form layers.
Stronger attractions between solute and solvent → more soluble.
Weak attractions between solute and solvent → not soluble.

runs.x: When a gas stove is lit, methane and oxygen from the air turn into carbon dioxide and water vapor, and the flame gives off heat and light. No new atoms appear. The atoms that were already there are rearranged into new substances.
Recall that chemical reactions are processes in which one set of substances is changed into another.
When a chemical reaction occurs, there will be an accompanying energy change.
Signs that a chemical reaction may have occurred:
A solid forms in a liquid (a precipitate).
The temperature changes, or light is given off.

Chemists around the world need a way to describe a reaction so that anyone can repeat it, whether they are making a medicine or testing a new battery. A chemical equation is that shared language. In one line it shows which substances react, which substances form and how many particles of each are involved, so it is the starting point for everything else in this unit.
We represent the change that takes place in a reaction using a chemical equation. The starting substances are known as reactants and the ending substances are known as products.
– symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulas and numbers.
– the starting substances in a chemical reaction.
– the ending substances in a chemical reaction.
– represents “yields” or “forms.” Shows the direction in which a chemical reaction proceeds.

Before chemists had formulas, reactions were described in words, and many lab procedures still start that way: “iron reacts with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide.” Turning a description into a word equation, and then into a chemical equation, is the first step in predicting how much of each substance is needed or produced.
– a description of a chemical reaction that uses the names of the reactants and products instead of their formulas.
Ex: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
The “+” is read as “and” (or “reacts with”). The arrow is read as “yields.”
A word equation does not show the formulas, the coefficients or the phases. A chemical equation shows all three.
Changing one small number in an equation can change everything. H
O is water that we drink, but H
is hydrogen peroxide, which is used as a bleach. Knowing the difference between the numbers that describe
particles react (coefficients) is the key to reading and balancing equations correctly.
When reading a chemical equation, there are two important numbers to take note of:
– large numbers placed in front of a chemical formula. Indicate the number of molecules or formula units (or moles) of a substance taking part in the reaction.
– small numbers placed to the bottom right of an element. Indicate the number of atoms of an element in a molecule or compound.
No coefficient means 1. No subscript means 1 atom.
For ionic compounds, one unit of the formula is called a
(ionic compounds do not form molecules). Ex: 3NaCl means 3 formula units of NaCl.
A subscript after parentheses multiplies every atom inside the parentheses. Ex: Ca(OH)

O contains 3 × 2 = 6 H atoms and 3 × 1 = 3 O atoms.

runs.x: When wood burns, the ashes weigh much less than the log. The “missing” mass did not disappear: it left as carbon dioxide and water vapor. If every product is captured, the total mass never changes.
– mass (matter) cannot be created or destroyed.
In any chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants must be equal to the total mass of the products.

Not every quantity in a reaction is easy to measure. The mass of a gas that escapes into the air, for example, cannot be placed on a balance. Because mass is conserved, a chemist who knows every other mass in the reaction can calculate the missing one, which is how scientists track the carbon dioxide released by burning fuels.
Since mass can be neither created nor destroyed, we can predict the amount of a substance that is consumed or produced in a chemical reaction.
Steps to Calculating a Missing Mass:
Create an algebraic equation by writing the mass of the given reactants and products.
Set the mass of the reactants equal to the mass of the products. Think of the arrow like an “equal sign.”

Why is mass conserved? The answer is found at the particle level. During a reaction, bonds break and new bonds form, but the atoms themselves are only rearranged. Counting the atoms of each element on both sides of an equation shows that the same atoms are present before and after, which is why the total mass never changes.
total number and type of atoms remains the same
before and after a chemical reaction.
Although the number of atoms of each element must remain the same, the number of molecules (or moles) does not necessarily need to.
mass is conserved because atoms are conserved. Every atom of the reactants ends up in the products, and each atom keeps its mass.

Every reaction involves an energy change. A burning candle gives off heat and light, and an instant cold pack pulls heat out of your hand. In both cases energy is not created or destroyed: it is converted between chemical potential energy and heat. This idea explains where the energy from fuels and food comes from and where it goes.
– energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted into different forms.
If there is a difference in the potential energy of the reactants and products, that energy will be released or absorbed as light, heat, etc.
Ex: when methane burns, the chemical potential energy stored in its bonds is converted into heat and light. The energy given off equals the potential energy lost by the chemicals.

When metals react, electrons move from one atom to another. Batteries and corrosion both depend on this electron transfer. No matter how the electrons move, they are never lost or created, so the total charge before a reaction must equal the total charge after it, just as mass and energy are conserved.
– charge cannot be created or destroyed.
Charge can be transferred from one object or particle to another as electrons are passed back and forth.

Heat always flows from the hotter object to the colder object, until both reach the same temperature.

Fortunately, most reactions follow a small number of patterns. Recognizing the pattern of a reaction allows a chemist to predict its products before ever running it in the lab.
Chemical reactions can be classified into 5 different types:
Each type has a pattern. In the patterns below, A and B stand for elements or positive ions, and X and Y stand for negative ions or the elements they come from.

Building complex substances from simpler ones is one of the main jobs of chemistry. The ammonia in fertilizer that helps feed billions of people is made by combining nitrogen and hydrogen, and rust forms as iron slowly combines with oxygen. Each of these is a synthesis reaction, in which simpler substances join to form one more complex product.
– chemical reaction in which two or more simple reactants combine into a more complex product.

Breaking compounds apart is just as important as building them. Airbags inflate in a fraction of a second when a solid compound decomposes into nitrogen gas, and metals such as aluminum are obtained by breaking down their compounds with electricity. In a decomposition reaction, one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.
– a chemical reaction in which a single reactant is broken down (decomposed) into two or more simple products.
Often energy (heat or electricity) must be added to break down a compound.

Some elements are reactive enough to push another element out of a compound. Copper wire placed in a silver nitrate solution slowly grows crystals of silver, and the same idea is used to recover valuable metals from solutions. In a single replacement reaction, one element takes the place of another element in a compound.
– a chemical reaction in which one element exchanges places with another element in a compound.

Mixing two clear solutions can suddenly produce a cloudy solid. Water treatment plants use this kind of reaction to remove harmful metal ions from drinking water. In a double replacement reaction, the ions of two compounds trade partners, and a new solid, water or a gas can form.
– a chemical reaction in which an ion in one compound is exchanged with an ion in another compound.
In double replacement reactions, positive ions replace positive ions, and negative ions replace negative ions.

Most of the energy used to heat homes, generate electricity and power cars comes from combustion. Engineers who design airbags and scuba tanks need to know how much space a gas will take up. Because every gas follows Avogadro’s law, one number describes the volume of a mole of any gas at standard conditions.

It is often helpful to know the volume that a gas will take up at standard temperature and pressure (STP: 273 K and 1 atm). This is known as the molar volume at STP.
Molar Volume of an Ideal Gas (at STP)
1 mole of an ideal gas will take up 22.4 liters of volume at STP.
The Reference Table lists this equivalence: 1 mole = 22.4 L (ideal gas at STP).

Many reactions produce or use gases, from the oxygen we breathe to the carbon dioxide that inflates bread dough. Converting between moles and volume lets chemists predict how much space a gas will fill.
To convert from moles to volume (at STP), multiply by 22.4 L.
To convert from volume (at STP) to moles, divide by 22.4 L.

runs.x: Car engines are tuned so that fuel and air mix in just the right ratio. Too little air, and some fuel goes unburned and pollutes; too much, and the engine loses power. In almost every real reaction, one reactant runs out before the other, and that reactant decides how much product can form.

Since substances must react in specific mole ratios given by the balanced chemical equation, if random amounts of 2 reactants are combined, there is a high chance that one substance will be completely consumed before the other.
– reactant that is completely used up and therefore restricts how much product is formed.
– reactant that is left over after the reaction is finished.

Imagine that you are making hamburgers at a barbecue. Each burger requires 2 buns and 1 patty. Buns come in packages of 12 while patties come in packages of 3. You will only be able to make 3 burgers, leaving you with 6 leftover buns.
The patties are the limiting reagent, since they are completely used up.
The buns are the excess reagent, since some are left over.
Steps to Determine Limiting and Excess Reagents:
Make sure the chemical equation is balanced.
Convert the starting amount of every reactant to moles.
Using mole ratios, convert the moles of every reactant into moles of one of the products.
The reactant that yields the smaller amount of product is the limiting reagent. The reactant that yields the larger amount of product is the excess reagent.
